title: The Manager Who Never Got the Manual
author: Ghassan Karian
summary: Ghassan Karian argues that management is the job with the greatest influence on wellbeing, productivity and retention but the least formal preparation. Drawing on DDI's Global Leadership Forecast 2025, DDI's HR Insights Report and Gartner's 2024 survey, he shows trust in immediate managers falling from 46 percent to 29 percent and only 20 percent of organisations having ready successors for critical roles. He describes the accidental manager cycle, in which excellent individual contributors are promoted without preparation, under-developed managers fail to develop their people, and the pipeline empties. He argues that lectures and seminars used alone do not work, while peer challenge, coaching and realistic practice do. He also says development comes too late, after promotion rather than before, and that the stress and expanded scope of managers is rational overwhelm rather than complaint.
points: Trust in immediate managers fell from 46 percent in 2022 to 29 percent in 2024, and 40 percent of stressed leaders have considered leaving management.
Most managers are promoted for excellence at another job, and 76 percent of organisations that prioritise internal promotion do not systematically assess leadership potential first.
Lectures, seminars and formal programmes used alone showed negative effects, while peer challenge, sustained coaching and realistic practice scenarios work better.
High-potential employees are far more likely to leave when their manager does not invest in their development.
Management scope has expanded to wellbeing, digital transformation and AI transition without added training, time or resources.
quotes: There is a job in almost every organisation that combines the highest direct influence on employee wellbeing, team productivity, and talent retention with some of the least investment in formal preparation.
Most people who enter management do so because they were excellent at something else (engineering, sales, finance, medicine, law) and the organisation’s answer to their excellence was promotion.

The causal chain is clear: under-developed managers do not develop their people; under-developed people leave; the pipeline empties; the organisation promotes the next person who happens to be excellent at the wrong thing; the cycle restarts.
The gap between stated ambition and operational reality is not 5 or 10 percentage points. It is the difference between a talent strategy and a talent prayer.
Structured peer challenge, sustained coaching from qualified practitioners, and repeated exposure to realistic high-stakes scenarios

leadership development often fails by teaching theory without providing safe spaces to apply new skills. The solution is not more content. It is practice environments that allow managers to build capability without the full cost of error.
Seventy-six percent of organisations that prioritise internal promotion do not systematically assess leadership potential before promoting. They assess past performance in a different job.
The management development data does not describe a soft HR problem. It describes the primary mechanism through which organisations convert their talent into their outputs.
